ch07.title: Evening at Capernaum
ch07.b002: On the evening of Tuesday, January 13, A.D. 28, they reached Capernaum. As always, Zebedee’s house in Bethsaida became their headquarters. Peter’s own house stood only a few steps away, and the moment he came near it his children ran out and he gathered them all into his arms at once. He had been gone almost a year. The children had grown in the meantime, and around his wife’s eyes there was a fine new line he did not recognize. Amatha, his wife’s mother, stood in the kitchen doorway to welcome her son-in-law. That night the company lodged at Zebedee’s house, but before he lay down Peter stood a long while at his own door, looking in at the sleeping children under the roof he had not slept beneath in so many months.
ch07.b003: The news that the Master was back spread through the city almost at once. Early the next morning Mary, his mother, hurried off to Nazareth. She was going, she said, to visit her son Joseph. Peter tilted his head when he heard it. On the very day her eldest son came home, the mother left for another son? John offered no explanation. Peter remembered the tears in the boat on the beach a year before, and asked nothing more.
ch07.b004: From Wednesday through Friday the Master stayed at Zebedee’s house, preparing the apostles for the great public preaching tour that was soon to begin. Earnest inquirers came to him, some alone and some in groups. Through Andrew he arranged to speak in the synagogue on the coming Sabbath.
ch07.b005: On Friday morning, as the Master was teaching by the sea, the crowd pressed him so close to the water’s edge that he signaled to some fishermen in a boat nearby, climbed in, and taught the people from the water for more than two hours. The boat’s name was *Simon*. It had once been Peter’s fishing boat, and the Master had built it with his own hands. That morning David Zebedee and two of his partners were using it. They had fished all night, caught nothing, and come in to wash and mend their nets.
ch07.b006: When the teaching was over, the Master told David that since he had lost time helping him, now he would help David: let them put out into the deep and let down the nets. David’s partner Simon answered that they had toiled all night for nothing, but at the Master’s word they would go—for David had given him a nod. When they let down the nets, the catch was so great the nets seemed ready to tear. They waved to their partners on the shore, and three boats were filled nearly to sinking. Then this Simon fell down at the Master’s knees and begged him to depart, for he was a sinful man. From that day David Zebedee, Simon, and their partners left their nets and followed the Master.
ch07.b007: Peter heard the story told over and over that evening. People called it a miracle. At first Peter believed so too. It did not occur to him that the Master was a fisherman who knew the ways of the fish in that lake better than anyone, and had simply known where they gathered at that hour of the day. What Peter held on to was something else. In his own old boat, the boat the Master’s hands had shaped and fitted, a man who bore his own name had gone down on his knees. *Leave me, for I am a sinner.* Peter said the words over to himself. He had a sudden foreboding that one day he too would say something like that. He shook his head to be rid of the feeling.
ch07.b009: At the synagogue meeting that Thursday evening, Andrew had taught on “The New Way.” On the Sabbath morning Peter preached on “The Kingdom,” and in the afternoon the Master preached on the will of the Father in heaven. At that time there were more believers in Capernaum than in any other city on earth.
ch07.b010: Matthew Levi stood at the back of the synagogue beside a pillar. In the years when he sat at the customs table, he had never been easy coming into this building; he could feel people’s eyes boring into his back. Out of old habit he stood at the back again today. The Master read one passage from the law and one from the prophet Isaiah—the passage that bids the people arise and shine. Then he spoke about religion as the experience of each single person.
ch07.b011: A good father, the Master said, loves his family as a whole precisely because he loves each member of it. From now on they were to come to the Father not as children of Israel but as children of God. As a people they were children of Israel; one by one, each of them was a child of God. The prophets had taught that God loves Israel, but he had come to proclaim a greater truth: that God loves each one of them. Jeremiah and Ezekiel had already seen it, he said, when they foretold a day when children’s teeth would no longer be set on edge because their fathers had eaten sour grapes.
ch07.b012: Matthew leaned his back against the pillar and could not steady his breathing. As one of the children of Israel he had long ago been cast out—a publican’s son, a collector of Roman money. His people had rejected him and the synagogue had shunned him. But this man was speaking not of a nation but of persons, one by one. Of one Matthew. He looked around him. The rich merchant in the front row, the poor widow, the tax collector by the back pillar—before God, each was one. At the close of his sermon the Master said that hate is the shadow of fear and revenge the mask of cowardice, and that man is a son of God, not a child of the devil. Matthew never forgot a word of it. Years later, when he gathered his notes of the Master’s sayings, the words of this Sabbath must surely have been among them.
ch07.b013: The moment the sermon ended, a young man in the congregation was seized by a violent epileptic fit and cried out. When the fit passed, he murmured as if in a dream, asking whether Jesus of Nazareth had come to destroy them. The Master quieted the people, took the young man by the hand, and told him to come out of it, and he woke at once. He was not possessed; he suffered from ordinary epilepsy, and his illness itself was not cured until after sundown that day. But he and the whole congregation believed it was the work of an evil spirit. The rumor ran through the city on the Sabbath wind: the Master had cast out a demon and healed a man by a miracle in the synagogue.
ch07.b014: On their way back from the synagogue they stopped at Peter’s house. Amatha, Peter’s mother-in-law, had lain sick with chills and fever for several days. Just about the time the Master stood over her, holding her hand, smoothing her brow, and speaking words of comfort, the fever happened to leave her. The Master had not yet had time to explain that what had happened in the synagogue was no miracle. Some of the apostles, remembering the water and the wine at Cana, seized on this as another miracle and rushed out to spread the news through the city. Matthew stayed in the doorway, watching them go. He was a keen reader of men. At the customs table he had seen, more times than he could count, how people hear only what they want to hear. Were those feet running into the street not feet of that kind? But he said nothing of this to anyone.
ch07.b016: As that Sabbath drew toward evening, Capernaum and all the villages around were seething with talk of miracles. The law forbade setting out even in search of healing during the Sabbath hours. So the sick and their families waited for the sun to set. One man, the instant he saw the sun go down behind his neighbor’s house, lifted his paralyzed daughter onto his back and started out.
ch07.b017: At Zebedee’s house supper was being made ready. The cooking and housework there were mostly in the hands of Peter’s wife and her mother. Philip stood beside the kitchen counting the loaves—thirteen men and a few guests, the same sum he always did. Tonight there was plenty. He tied the sack shut, satisfied. The sun had just set. They were sitting around the table, still breaking bread, when Peter’s wife heard strange sounds in the front yard and went to open the door.
ch07.b018: The yard was full of people. The road from Capernaum was covered with people as far as she could see. She ran to her husband, and Peter went to tell the Master. The Master stepped out through the front door. Philip followed him and stopped on the threshold.
ch07.b019: He was a man who counted, so he counted first. A hundred, two hundred, five hundred. The counting broke down. There were nearly a thousand. Not all of them were sick. Some carried stretchers, some carried children on their backs, some held up aged parents. In the front rows were the blind, the lame, people whose skin was white and peeling. Groans and weeping and the calling of names mingled together. A few torches were lit, and faces swayed in their light. Never in his life had Philip seen so much suffering in one place. This was not something to be reckoned in loaves of bread. For the first time he understood how small his reckoning was.
ch07.b020: Someone in the yard cried out to the Master to speak the word—to restore their health, heal their diseases, and save their souls. Peter begged the Master to answer their plea. Philip watched the Master’s face. There was something in it he had never seen before: deep compassion, and something else holding that compassion steady. Looking down on the crowd, the Master began to say that he had come to reveal the Father and establish the kingdom; and so, if it were the will of the One who sent him and not at odds with his work of proclaiming the kingdom, he would desire to see his children made whole—but the rest of his words were lost in the tumult.
ch07.b021: What happened next, Philip was never able to describe exactly as long as he lived. Something passed through the yard. It was not wind. It was not sound. Only, at that moment, somewhere a crutch dropped to the ground. Someone burst into tears; someone else screamed. In the torchlight, shadows rose up from stretchers. Names were being called everywhere. Six hundred and eighty-three men, women, and children were made whole on the spot. Such a sight had never been seen on earth before, and has not been seen since.
ch07.b022: Philip stood clinging to the doorpost. *Show us.* All his life that had been his word, and the Master had always patiently shown him. But what he saw tonight was something he had never asked for, and something larger than he could bear. He was weeping. He did not know when he had begun. Beside him Matthew was gazing at the faces in the yard. Some of them he knew—men who had glared at him across the customs table. Now they were holding each other and weeping. Matthew could not take his eyes off them. And then, suddenly, he looked at the Master’s face. It was not the face of a man rejoicing. It was the face of a man more astonished than anyone there.
ch07.b023: The Master Nowhere to Be Found
ch07.b024: That night Zebedee’s house overflowed with people beside themselves with joy. The apostles’ excitement knew no bounds. Never before or after did their hopes rise so high. Only days before, had the Master not told them that the hour had come to proclaim the kingdom with power? They believed that promise had been fulfilled today. If this was only the beginning, what was still to come? Whatever doubts had lingered were swept away. Peter went about the yard clapping strangers on the shoulder, and Simon Zelotes grabbed someone and shouted that the kingdom had come.
ch07.b025: Amatha, Peter’s mother-in-law, was truly healed that night too. The fever that had broken in the afternoon had only happened to subside; but some hours after sundown, together with what took place in the yard, her illness really left her. She threw off her blankets and tried to go to the kitchen, and Peter’s wife, aghast, held her back. Peter watched the two women wrangling and laughed out loud. Tonight anything could make him laugh.
ch07.b026: But the Master was nowhere to be seen. Those who had been healed waited late into the night to thank him. The apostles searched the house inside and out. The Master was nowhere. As the hours passed, cracks began to show in Peter’s joy. Why, on a night like this? If only he were here, the joy would be complete.
ch07.b027: The hour was late when the Master returned. Most of those who had been healed had already gone home. When the apostles and the others who remained tried to greet him with congratulations, he refused them. They should not rejoice, he said, that the Father had power to heal the body, but that he was mighty to save the soul. Then he said only that they should go to their rest, for tomorrow they must be about the Father’s business.
ch07.b028: The twelve went to bed disappointed and bewildered. Hardly any of them slept, except the twins. It seemed that no sooner had the Master lifted their spirits than he shattered their hopes. In the darkness Peter heard the breathing of Andrew lying beside him. His brother was awake too. They were both thinking the same thing: *We cannot understand him. What does this mean?*
ch07.b030: Peter spoke it into the dark.
ch07.b032: Andrew answered. He already knew what Peter had been about to ask.
ch07.b034: Peter never did sleep. Long before dawn, discovering that the Master had left the house, he woke James and John, and the three of them groped their way out in the dark to find him. After searching more than an hour, they found him in one of the places where he liked to pray. Peter asked him straight out why, when everyone was so overjoyed, he alone seemed troubled by the great healing.
ch07.b035: For more than four hours the Master tried to explain to the three of them what had happened and the dangers of such events—why the Father’s kingdom could not be built on wonders and bodily healing, and why he had come out to pray. He had been asking for wisdom, he told them, so that he would not let all his time be swallowed up in caring for bodily suffering until the work of the spirit was neglected. Peter listened hard. But he did not understand. How could people being healed be a danger? He thought of the faces in the yard, holding each other and weeping. How could those faces be a danger?
ch07.b036: Meanwhile, as the sun came up, people began crowding around Zebedee’s house again. The sick and the curious clamored to see the Master. Andrew and the apostles did not know what to do. The twins, looking as fresh as if they had slept soundly all night, kept the gate and made room in a corner of the yard for those carrying stretchers. They did not ask what all this commotion meant. When people came, you made room for them; that was their work. Simon Zelotes stepped out before the crowd and began to talk to them. Matthew stood beside him and watched. Simon was good at calming a crowd. His voice was loud and rough, but this morning he was speaking not of the sword but of patience. Matthew thought of how much the man had changed in a single year. Meanwhile Andrew set out with several others to find the Master.
ch07.b037: When Andrew reached the hillside, he asked the Master why he had left them alone with the crowd. Everyone was looking for him; never had so many sought his teaching. Would he not come back and minister to them? The Master answered that his mission was to reveal the Father and proclaim the kingdom. Why had these people come now? Was it not because their bodies had been healed, rather than because they had received the truth? He had told the apostles to care for the sick, but he could not let healing crowd out his teaching. They were to go back and tell the people to believe what they had been taught and to rejoice in the liberty of the sons of God, and then make ready to leave at once for the other cities of Galilee.
ch07.b038: Andrew and the apostles went down with heavy hearts, sent the crowd away, and packed. Peter stopped in the middle of his packing. He was no great hand at figures, but this time he reckoned. At least a thousand people could have been baptized into the kingdom today. And they were leaving those thousand behind. Even after they were on the road, he begged the Master again and again to turn back. So did the others. The Master listened to them patiently to the end. But he would not let them return.
ch07.b039: For a while no one said a word. Then Thomas spoke up.
ch07.b040: “Come on, let’s go! The Master has decided. We may not grasp all the mysteries of the kingdom, but one thing is plain enough—the teacher we follow is not out for his own glory.”
ch07.b041: Peter turned to look at Thomas—the man who always argued against everything first, the man of gloom and doubt. Now that same Thomas was the first to move. Peter swallowed the thousand that stuck in his throat. *A teacher not out for his own glory.* He saw again the face that had turned away the congratulations in the yard last night. That face weighed more than a thousand baptisms. He took his first step. On the afternoon of Sunday, January 18, A.D. 28, they set out reluctantly for Rimmon. It was the first truly open and public preaching tour of the cities of Galilee.
ch07.b042: Not long after they had gone, the Master’s brothers James and Jude came to Zebedee’s house. Around noon that day Jude had sought out his brother James and urged him to come with him to see Jesus, but by the time James finally agreed, it was too late. The Master was gone. In the yard nothing remained but the trampled earth where the crowds of the night before had stood.
ch07.b044: The tour lasted about two months. John’s former apostles went with them. Each of the Master’s apostles had one of John’s apostles as his partner, and Abner was paired with Andrew. This time the Master placed almost no restrictions on them—only that they stay away from Nazareth and be discreet when passing through Capernaum and Tiberias. The apostles were overjoyed to be free at last to preach as they liked.
ch07.b045: Rimmon was a small city that had once worshiped Ramman, a Babylonian god of the air. There Peter preached on Aaron and the golden calf, one of the great sermons of his early years. The title alone told you the story: a people who could not wait for the unseen God and made themselves a god they could see. Matthew nodded along as he listened, and then caught himself. He thought of themselves only days before, begging for wonders, pleading to turn back. Did Peter realize that? Looking at Peter’s flushed face, Matthew thought he probably did not. And he thought that this was very like Peter.
ch07.b046: At Jotapata, on the second evening, Nathaniel said he was confused about the Master’s teaching on prayer, thanksgiving, and worship. The Master answered him at length. God has forgiven us even before we think to ask, he said, but that forgiveness becomes real in our own experience only when we forgive our fellow men. Matthew lingered over those words. He was a man who had been forgiven. He had been forgiven ever since the day he stood up from the customs table. But had he truly forgiven those who had despised him? He still longed to let them know how much he was giving. Was that forgiveness, or only another kind of bookkeeping?
ch07.b047: At Ramah the Master talked a long while with an aged Greek philosopher who taught that science and philosophy were enough to satisfy human need. The Master listened patiently and granted the truth of much that he said. The apostles were disconcerted. Afterward the Master told them that genuine inward certainty does not fear outward examination, and that intolerance is a mask over secret doubts about one’s own belief. On the second evening Thomas asked how a new believer could be sure of the truth of the kingdom. The Master told him that though they could not watch the spirit at work within them, there was a practical way to tell how far they had yielded to it: by the measure of their love for their fellow men.
ch07.b048: Philip slapped his knee when he heard that. The spirit cannot be seen. But love can. Who hands the bread to someone else first, who shoulders a tired man’s load, who covers for another’s mistake. That he could see. That night, lying in bed, he called up his companions’ faces one by one: the twins sitting silently beside Thomas on his dark days; Nathaniel, who would leave any council and run when trouble came to his family; Andrew, lifting up his exhausted brothers one by one. For the first time Philip realized that his eyes, which had only ever asked to be shown, had in fact been seeing something every day.
ch07.b049: All through the tour Matthew was never free of worry about money. The villages were poor and offerings were few, and twenty-four men had to eat. Each night he handed over what had come in to Judas, who kept the purse, and no small part of it came from Matthew’s own pocket, given in the names of other believers. In Zebulun the people were of mixed blood, hardly Jew or gentile, and though they had heard of the healings at Capernaum, few of them believed. That week Matthew put in twice his usual share. No one knew. Only let the Master know, he prayed silently once again.
ch07.b051: Iron had great mines. While the apostles went from house to house and preached in the public places, the Master spent nearly all his time in the mines, working with the miners, for he had never before shared a miner’s life. Each evening Philip met the Master as he came back to their lodging. His face and hands were gray with stone dust, and there was grit in his hair. Philip brought him water and looked at those hands. They were the hands that had been raised before a thousand people on that night in Capernaum. Today they had hauled rock in a dark shaft. Philip could not make sense of it. But he knew that he had never once seen anything small or grudging in those hands.
ch07.b052: Late in the afternoon of the third day, as the Master was walking back from the mines through a narrow side street, a leper came out of a wretched hovel and knelt in front of him. If the Master only would, he said, he could make him clean; he had heard the message of the Master’s disciples, and if only he could be made clean, he would enter the kingdom of heaven. A leper could not go to the synagogue or take part in public worship, and this man sincerely believed he could never be received into the kingdom unless he was cleansed. The Master looked at him, and the man pressed his face to the ground. The Master reached out his hand, touched him, and said that he was willing; let him be clean. And at once he was healed.
ch07.b053: The Master raised him to his feet and told him to say nothing to anyone, but to go quietly about his business, show himself to the priest, and offer the gifts Moses had commanded. But the man did not do it. He went all through the town crying out that Jesus had cured his leprosy. Everyone in the village knew him, so no one doubted it. The next morning the Master was so mobbed by the sick that he had to leave the town early. He never entered it again, though he stayed two more days on the outskirts near the mines, teaching the miners who believed. This was the first so-called miracle the Master had performed by his own deliberate intention up to that time.
ch07.b054: Philip could understand the man. He had seen, and so he wanted to tell. A man who asks to be shown wants, once he has seen, to show others. Philip himself was like that—as on the day he told Nathaniel to come and see. Yet the Master had said to tell no one. Philip paced back and forth between those two for a long while. Was it wrong to show? Or was the question what one showed? For the first time Philip asked himself what he ought to put into his own words, *come and see*.
ch07.b055: From Iron they went to Gischala for two days, then to Chorazin for almost a week. Chorazin received them coldly. In no place where the Master had taught had he met with such general rejection. The apostles were deeply discouraged, and Andrew and Abner had a hard time keeping their companions’ spirits up. In the market at Chorazin Peter shouted himself hoarse, and people turned their backs and went their way. Each evening he ate his supper in silence. The thousand at Capernaum swam before his eyes. There, people had shoved their way in to reach him; here, no one so much as looked at him. He knew what made the difference, and knowing it only made it worse. They passed quietly through Capernaum and went on to Madon, where they fared little better. Most of the apostles privately believed that things were going so badly because the Master would not let them speak of him as a healer. How they longed for him to cleanse one more leper, or in some other way show his power! The Master did not waver.
ch07.b057: When the Master said that tomorrow they would go to Cana, the apostles’ spirits lifted. He was well known there. On the third day Titus, a prominent citizen of Capernaum, came hurrying into Cana. He was a partial believer, and his son was dying. Matthew knew that face. In his customs days, whenever that household’s wagons went by, he had written large sums in his ledger. And now that proud man, covered in the dust of the road, was clinging to the Master, begging him to come to Capernaum and heal his son.
ch07.b058: The apostles held their breath. Was the thing they had been waiting for finally about to happen? Matthew saw the face of Judas, standing beside him, light up. Judas had grown quieter since Chorazin. *This time, surely,* his face said. But at the Master’s first words that face went rigid. Matthew remembered that rigid face for a long time. It was the face of a man who had been waiting for something and was folding his waiting away once more. The Master looked at the father and asked how long he must bear with them; the power of God was in their midst, yet unless they saw signs and wonders they would not believe. Titus said that he did believe, but begged the Master to come before the child died. The Master bowed his head a moment in silence, and then told him to go home: his son would live. Titus believed him and hurried back. On the way his servants came out to meet him with the news that the boy was alive. When he asked at what hour the boy had begun to mend, they said the fever had left him about the seventh hour of the day before. It was the very hour the Master had said, *your son will live*. Titus and his whole household believed. Even the apostles took it for a miracle. But it was not a miracle of healing the body. It was foreknowledge of how nature would take its course.
ch07.b059: When Cana was stirred into an uproar, they hurried on to Nain. A great crowd of believers and curious people followed them, bent on seeing wonders. Near the gate of the town they met a funeral procession. A respected widow of Nain had lost her only son, and half the village was walking with her to the burial ground. The widow and her friends recognized the Master and begged him to bring the boy back to life. The Master went up, lifted the cover of the bier, and examined the boy. He found that the boy was not really dead. He told the mother not to weep; her son was not dead but sleeping, and would be given back to her. Then he took the youth by the hand and told him to wake and rise. The boy sat up and began to speak.
ch07.b060: The crowd went wild. Some trembled with fear, some were struck senseless, some wailed over their sins. The Master told them again and again that the boy had not been dead, but it was no use. People took it for his modest way of hiding a miracle. Peter took it that way too that night. He wanted to believe the Master’s words. But his eyes had seen a boy sit up on a bier. The dead had been raised. That was what he believed, and he was glad to believe it. The Master never managed to make even his apostles fully understand. He did persuade them, however, to leave the episode out of their later records; only Luke, who wrote it down as it had been told to him, preserved it.
ch07.b061: Early the next day they left for Endor, where for a few days they rested away from the crowds. The Master told them again the story of King Saul and the witch of Endor, and explained that the spirits of the dead do not come back to speak with the living. After two days of rest the Master said that tomorrow they would go back to Capernaum. By now, he said, the people there would have partly recovered from all the excitement.
ch07.b062: On the evening of March 17 they came into Capernaum. Matthew walked at the very back of the company. The sun was going down behind the hills across the lake. As they passed the customs house he slowed his steps. At the table where he used to sit, a stranger sat counting coins. Matthew looked at the man a long while. Two months ago, on just such an evening, six hundred and eighty-three people had risen to their feet in a yard in this city. How many of them were now in the kingdom? Matthew was a man who counted people, and he knew the number would not be large. And it occurred to him that this might be why the Master’s face had not been a rejoicing face that night. Bodies had risen in an instant, but souls do not rise that way. Matthew himself was proof of it. He had stood up from the customs table in a single day, but the rising of his soul still needed a step every day. He took his eyes from the man at the table and walked on after the backs of the eleven ahead of him, toward Zebedee’s house. In its yard the evening lamps were being lit, one by one.
ch07.b064: The events follow Papers 145 and 146: the arrival on January 13, Mary’s departure for Nazareth, and the synagogue arrangements (145:0.1–0.2); the boat named Simon, David Zebedee’s catch, the kneeling Simon, and the explanation that it was no miracle (145:1.1–1.3); the synagogue sermons of Andrew, Peter, and Jesus, the teaching on personal religion, the epileptic young man, and Amatha’s fever and her healing after sundown (145:2.1–2.17); the crowd at sundown, the man with the paralyzed daughter, Peter’s wife at the door, and the healing of 683 (145:3.1–3.15); Jesus’ absence and the disappointment that night (145:4.1–4.3); the dawn prayer and the three apostles, Simon Zelotes addressing the crowd, Andrew’s plea and Jesus’ refusal, the departure of January 18, the late visit of Jesus’ brothers, Peter’s reckoning, and Thomas’s words (145:5.1–5.10); the two-month tour and the pairing of apostles (146:0.1–0.2, 146:3.9); Peter’s sermon at Rimmon (146:1.1); Nathaniel’s question at Jotapata (146:2.1–2.18); the philosopher and Thomas’s question at Ramah (146:3.1–3.8); Zebulun (146:3.11); the mines of Iron and the leper (146:4.1–4.5); discouragement at Gischala, Chorazin, and Madon (146:4.6); Titus at Cana (146:5.1–5.3); the widow’s son at Nain (146:6.1–6.4); Endor and the return (146:7.1–7.3).
ch07.b065: Character facts come from Paper 139: Peter’s family and mother-in-law (139:2.1); Philip’s “show me,” his stewardship, his gift of “come,” and his admiration for Jesus’ generosity (139:5.2–5.8); Matthew’s customs past, his secret gifts to the apostolic funds, his insight into men, and his later notes (139:7.1–7.9); Thomas’s “Let’s go!” (139:8.8).
ch07.b066: Fiction has been added in the apostles’ inner thoughts and feelings, weather and landscape, Peter’s homecoming, Peter’s brooding over the confession of the fisherman who shared his name, Matthew standing at the back of the synagogue, Philip counting loaves before meeting the crowd and the sounds and shadows of the healing, the brief night exchange between Peter and Andrew, the tone of Simon Zelotes’ words to the crowd, the Master’s appearance on returning from the mines, Matthew’s recognizing Titus, Amatha trying to get up, Judas’s face at the Titus episode, and the closing scene at the customs house (the text says only that they returned on March 17). The text does not say how much Matthew gave on this tour; his secret giving follows the character described in 139:7.8–7.9. The apostles who ran to spread the news after the synagogue incident are left, as in the text, as “some.”
ch07.b067: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
